title: Dear Alpha School: I Hope You're Right
author: The Next 30 Years
summary: An open letter from an education writer who spent a year inside Success Academy to Alpha School founders MacKenzie Price and Joe Liemandt. The author wants Alpha's claims—students learning in two hours a day, 2.6 times faster than expected—to be true, but argues the company's triumphalist rhetoric and restricted data access undermine the case. Extraordinary results invite the same questions they always have: who are the students, how is 'expected growth' defined, and will results hold outside a $40k-a-year private setting? The ask isn't a randomized trial—just enough transparency that independent researchers can evaluate the conclusions rather than the marketing. School, the author reminds Alpha, is not merely a content-delivery system; it is a cultural habit generations of families have found valuable for reasons that go beyond measurable academic outcomes.
points: Alpha's 2.6x faster learning claim remains unverifiable because researchers cannot independently reconstruct how the figure was derived or test alternative explanations.

The rhetoric that dismisses traditional schools as 'factory' models producing 'compliant citizens' causes thoughtful educators to stop listening—not from defensiveness, but because dismissiveness signals misunderstanding.
School is a cultural habit, not merely an academic delivery system; families value what schools are, not just what they teach—and Alpha's case must account for that.
Confidence attracts attention; humility attracts allies—the educational innovations that endure do so by inviting inspection, not demanding admiration.

Every dollar spent on marketing asking people to trust Alpha's conclusions is a dollar spent buying belief; every dollar enabling independent researchers to verify them is a dollar making belief unnecessary.
quotes: Extraordinary results invite two equal and opposite temptations: belief and disbelief. I try to resist both.
I want badly for this to be true, so let me be clear: this is not a “put up or shut up” challenge.

School is a cultural habit. It’s an enduring social practice that persists not because no one has thought to improve or replace it, but because generations of people have found value in gathering children together to learn alongside one another under the guidance of adults.
I’ll state it bluntly: confidence attracts attention; humility attracts allies.
The most persuasive and effective reformers eventually stop asking people to admire their vision and start inviting them to inspect their work.

every dollar you spend on marketing — podcasts, videos, and social media — asking people to trust your conclusions is a dollar spent buying belief. Every dollar spent enabling independent researchers to verify those conclusions is a dollar spent making belief unnecessary.
